title: Concession and contrast at C1
tagline: Give ground gracefully, then make your point — the connectors that raise the register.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations (MUCH, MATTER, ALBEIT, MAY, SAID)
Reading & Use of English Part 2 — open cloze (however, whilst, granted, admittedly)
Writing Part 1 — essay: conceding a counter-argument before making your case
Speaking Parts 3 and 4 — sounding balanced when you weigh up two sides of an issue
why: Concession is what separates a one-sided C1 essay from one that has clearly weighed the other side before arguing its own case. Use of English Part 4 regularly sets these connectors as key words, and Part 2's open cloze often tests the one word that introduces a concession in an academic text. Knowing which device takes a full clause and which takes only a phrase — and which register each belongs to — is exactly what examiners reward under 'range' and 'coherence'.

diagrams.title: From although to much as

before.text: Although I admire her ambition, I think she is taking on too much.

after.text: Much as I admire her ambition, I think she is taking on too much.

steps: Much as is followed by a full clause (subject + verb), exactly like although.
No change of word order is needed — only the connector changes, and the tone becomes more grudging.

diagrams.title: The inverted, literary pattern
diagrams.caption: Front the adjective or adverb, then add as or though — a compact, literary way to concede a point before making yours.

formula.ex: I respect his view / a lack of resources

head: Connector
Pattern
Example
rows: Much as I respect the decision, I think it was rushed.
However carefully you plan a field trip, something always goes wrong.
no matter + wh-word + clause, main clause
No matter how much revision you do, nerves still get the better of you.
Whilst the proposal has merit, the budget makes it unrealistic.
The trip was a success, albeit an exhausting one.
Granted, the museum was closed, but the walk through the old town made up for it.
for all + noun phrase, main clause
For all his experience, the guide still misjudged the weather on the trek.
Adj/Adv + as/though + S + V, main clause
Difficult as it was, Nadia finished the essay before midnight.

examples.text: Much as I enjoyed the debate, I still think the motion was poorly worded.
examples.note: grudging concession before the writer's real opinion

examples.text: Whilst the coastal route is more scenic, it adds two hours to the journey.
examples.note: whilst = while, but favoured in formal writing

use.point: Conceding with however, no matter how / what / who, and whatever

examples.text: However well you know Cusco, the altitude still catches you out.
No matter how hard the team trained, the final result was out of their hands.
Whatever the examiners decide, the school will appeal the result.
examples.note: whatever = it makes no difference what

use.point: Adding a concession after the point has already been made

examples.text: The internet connection in the village was patchy. Even so, the video call went ahead.
It rained for most of the excursion. All the same, nobody wanted to go home early.
examples.note: all the same, slightly more conversational than even so

examples.text: The lecture overran badly. That said, it was the most useful session of the week.
examples.note: that said, common in spoken and semi-formal register

use.point: Emphatic, literary concession: inversion and for all

examples.text: Tired as she was, Sofia stayed up to finish the mural for the festival.
Try as he might, Liam could not persuade the committee to change the date.
examples.note: try as + subject + might, a fixed pattern

examples.text: For all its reputation, the new app crashes constantly during exams.

watch_out.wrong: Much as I respect him, but I cannot agree.
watch_out.right: Much as I respect him, I cannot agree.
watch_out.why: Much as already signals the contrast; adding but as well duplicates the connector.

watch_out.wrong: However you are tired, finish the report.
watch_out.right: However tired you are, finish the report.
watch_out.why: However and the adjective or adverb must be fronted together, before the subject.

watch_out.wrong: Whilst I was in Arequipa, but the volcano was hidden in cloud.
watch_out.right: Whilst I was in Arequipa, the volcano was hidden in cloud.
watch_out.why: Whilst already carries the contrast on its own; no extra but is needed.

watch_out.wrong: The hike was hard, granted the views were spectacular.
watch_out.right: The hike was hard. Granted, the views were spectacular.
watch_out.why: Granted / admittedly opens its own sentence or clause; it cannot simply join two clauses like and.

watch_out.wrong: Albeit the trek was gruelling, we reached the summit.
watch_out.right: The trek was gruelling, albeit a rewarding one.
watch_out.why: Albeit is followed by an adjective, adverb or noun phrase, not a full finite clause.

watch_out.wrong: Difficult it was, Nadia kept going.
watch_out.right: Difficult as it was, Nadia kept going.
watch_out.why: The inverted pattern needs as (or though) immediately after the fronted adjective.

dialogue.title: Rehearsal week
dialogue.context: Miss Vega checks on the school play three days before the festival, and Mateo, Sofia, Liam and Nadia admit how far behind they really are.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: How's the play coming along? Be honest with me.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Much as I hate to admit it, we're behind schedule.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: However hard we rehearse, Liam still forgets act two.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: That's unfair — no matter how many times I read the script, the lines just vanish on stage.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Whilst that's true, the costumes are finally ready, so that's one problem solved.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Small mercies. What about the sound system?

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: It's still unreliable. Even so, we tested it twice yesterday and it held up both times.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: For all its problems, this is still the best set the school has ever built.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Tired as we all are, I honestly think we can pull this off by Friday.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Granted, we're cutting it close, but I'd rather finish strong than rush now.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: That's the spirit. One more full run tomorrow, then.

items.sentence: ___ the criticism, the director refused to change the ending.
items.why: for all + noun phrase means despite; 'despite of' is not standard English.

items.sentence: ___ hard you practise, stage fright never fully disappears.
items.why: no matter how + adjective + clause; 'no matter' alone needs a wh-word after it.

items.sentence: The plan was risky. ___, the team voted to go ahead.
items.why: even so links back to a fact already stated, in a new sentence.

items.sentence: ___ I understand your concerns, I still think we should proceed.
items.why: much as + clause (subject + verb) expresses grudging concession; albeit cannot introduce a full clause like this.

items.sentence: The show was chaotic backstage, ___ a memorable one.
items.why: albeit + adjective phrase follows the clause it qualifies.

items.sentence: ___, the rehearsal ran late, but everyone stayed until the end.
items.why: admittedly opens a sentence to concede a fact before the contrast that follows.

items.sentence: ___ she might, Sofia could not fix the microphone before the show.
items.why: try as + subject + might is a fixed pattern for a determined but unsuccessful attempt.

practice.instructions: Complete each sentence with one or two words so that it is grammatically correct.

items.sentence: Much ___ I admire her work ethic, I think she needs more rest.
___ carefully you word it, the email will upset someone.
The results were disappointing. ___, the coach praised the team's effort.
___ its flaws, the new library is a huge improvement on the old one.
The trek up to the ruins is exhausting, ___ genuinely unforgettable.
He ___ be the most talented player on the team, but he never turns up to practice on time.
Nervous ___ she was, Sofia delivered the speech without a single mistake.

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first, using the word given. Do not change the word given. Use between two and five words.

items.first: Although I admire her, I think she has taken on too much.
items.second_end: , I think she has taken on too much.

items.first: It doesn't matter how much you practise; stage fright never fully goes away.
items.second_end: you practise, stage fright never fully goes away.

items.first: The conference speakers were disappointing, yet the audience still enjoyed the networking session.
items.second_end: the audience still enjoyed the networking session.

items.first: Despite his experience, the guide still misjudged the weather on the trek.
items.second_end: the guide still misjudged the weather on the trek.

items.first: The trek was exhausting, but it was genuinely unforgettable.
He is undeniably talented, but he never turns up to rehearsals on time.
items.second_end: he never turns up to rehearsals on time.

summary: Front a concessive connector to concede a point before disagreeing: Much as I admire it, I can't agree.
However and no matter how/what/who need the adjective, adverb or wh-word fronted together with them.
Even so, all the same and that said add a concession as a separate sentence, after the fact has been stated.
Albeit and for all take a phrase, not a full clause; whilst and much as take a clause.
Save the inverted, literary forms — Tired as she was, Try as he might — for writing that wants extra weight.
